newsitem.title: THAILAND: Austerity policy sparks problems for Thai PM.
newsitem.headline: Austerity policy sparks problems for Thai PM.

text.p: Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's austerity policy has already created rifts in his coalition government less than two months after it was formed, politicians and analysts said on Thursday.
Chavalit and his ally, Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, say cutting spending is necessary to keep the current account deficit from ballooning and to put the slowing economy on a steadier footing.
Although their fiscal discipline has been lauded by economists and foreign investors, the reaction from some coalition politicians has been negative.
Representatives of at least two parties in his six-party coalition have attacked moves to delay or put on hold costly projects.

Decisions on two projects -- a new airport for Bangkok costing 100 billion baht ($3.88 billion) and the purchase of a 2.9 billion baht survey satellite from Canada -- have drawn particularly strong criticism.
The government gave the transport and communications ministry one month to come up with recommendations on the second airport, but decided at the same time to expand the existing Don Muang airport.

Amnuay said the Aviation Department had estimated it would take five to seven years before the second airport, that was originally due to be ready in 2000, was operational. Earthworks at the site would be costly.
Transport and Communications Minister Suwat Liptapallop said the main obstacle to the second airport was a lack of money and it would cost much less to expand Don Muang.
But Deputy Prime Minister Montri Pongpanich and Deputy Transport and Communications Minister Somsak Thepsutin, from a junior coalition group, the Social Action Party, questioned the airport decision.
"If the country is really facing that (financial ) problem, all new projects have to be suspended," Somsak said.

Montri said: "Amnuay exaggerated when he said that the sand to fill the land will cost 900 baht per cubic metre, and if the price he said was right the government should fire minister Somsak (Thepsutin)."

Last week Samak Sundaravej, Deputy Prime Minister and head of the Prachakorn Thai Party, another coalition partner, criticised Amnuay for apparent reluctance to approve the purchase of a survey satellite from Canada.
"Amnuay has used austerity without thinking of saving the face of the respective ministry that negotiated the project," said Samak. The contract was eventually signed.
Krikiat Phipatseritham, dean of Thailand's Chamber of Commerce University, said he expected the austerity policy to set off more coalition rifts.
"The rift has already emerged and it will snowball," he said.
